column1: Extending the Range of Robust PCE Inflation Measures

The thesis titled Extending the Range of Robust PCE Inflation Measures by Sergio Ocampo  Raphael Schoenle  and Dominic A. Smith  evaluates the forecasting performance of various robust inflation measures from 1970 to 2024  focusing on core  median  and trimmed mean personal-consumption-expenditure (PCE) inflation. The study finds that core inflation performs significantly worse than median and trimmed mean inflation in terms of forecasting accuracy. Among alternative trimmed mean measures  no single trim consistently outperforms others  as a wide range of trims produces statistically similar average errors. However  different trims suggest varying predictions for trend inflation within a range of 0.5 to 1 percentage points in any given month. This range and its midpoint are found to outperform all individual trimmed mean measures in tracking trend inflation  indicating that the range of inflation implied by near-optimal trims could serve as a valuable complement to any single inflation measure.

The study is motivated by the resurgence of high and volatile inflation post-2020 pandemic  which has increased the focus on inflation measures that indicate current and future trends. Core inflation  which excludes historically volatile categories like food and energy  is compared with median and trimmed mean measures that exclude categories with the highest and lowest inflation rates. These robust measures are crucial for central bankers to communicate inflation behavior. The paper re-evaluates these measures' forecasting performance against standard benchmarks and extends the analysis to alternative trimmed mean measures  covering several high-inflation episodes  including the 1970s and recent post-pandemic inflation.

The findings reveal that trimmed mean and median inflation measures outperform core inflation in terms of root-mean-square error (RMSE) against standard measures of current and future trend inflation. This result challenges the common focus on core inflation by central banks and aligns with previous studies that also found trimmed mean and median inflation superior. The study further explores the properties of trimmed mean inflation measures  finding no single best measure in terms of predictive performance. By constructing alternative trimmed mean inflation series and varying the shares of expenditure excluded  the study ranks these series based on their RMSEs compared to current and future trend inflation.

The analysis shows that official median and trimmed mean measures perform nearly as well as the best alternative robust measures across different periods and trend targets  despite the best trims varying significantly depending on the sample and whether the current or future inflation trend is targeted. For instance  the optimal trim for future trend inflation over the extended 1970 to 2024 sample is more aggressive than in any subsamples  while in the 2000-2024 period  trimming only 52 percent of expenditure is optimal. However  the RMSEs of official robust measures and the best alternative trimmed mean measures are statistically indistinguishable in most samples.

An important insight is that similarities in predictive performance obscure significant differences in the behavior of the series over time. The range between the levels of official robust inflation series is wide  averaging 0.48 percentage points before 2020 and growing to 0.67 percentage points from 2020 onward. This indicates that these measures often provide different signals about current and future inflation in any given month  while tracking the trend equally well only on average. The study suggests that using the range of inflation implied by near-optimal trims could be a valuable complement to any single inflation measure  providing a more comprehensive understanding of inflation trends.
